name: Salmon (Farmed)
notes:
Farmed Atlantic salmon, nutrition from USDA. Most of salmon's footprint is its feed: per kg of fillet about 0.69 kg fishmeal, 0.18 kg fish oil, 0.33 kg soy and 0.18 kg wheat. The fishmeal and oil are made from wild anchoveta, so salmon is charged with the wild fish killed to make its feed, as a direct kill. That's a large part of its sentient harm.

Emissions start from Poore & Nemecek's salmon total (~11.9 kg CO2e/kg). The feed share is counted through the feed rows, small pond methane and nitrous oxide are set from the literature, and the remaining ~4.2 kg is direct CO2 (farm energy and logistics). Land is only the feed cropland, much of it Brazilian soy.

No salmon brain has been counted. The ~110 million neurons are estimated from body size (4.5 kg) using a fish brain-scaling rule anchored on brown trout. The 4.5 kg weight has no recorded derivation.
land_types_note: Land is only the feed crops (soy, wheat, corn); much aquafeed soy comes from Brazil.

name: Tuna (Wild)
notes:
Wild-caught tuna (the main market species), nutrition from USDA. It's tagged 'wild', so the Over-Hunting slider divides its score.

There's no land, feed or methane. Emissions are almost all fishing-boat diesel: ~3.9 kg CO2 per kg, from Poore & Nemecek's wild-fish range (3–5.4), placed toward the high end because distant-water tuna fleets are fuel-hungry. A large 60 kg fish yields ~60% edible meat, so relatively few animals die per kg.

No tuna brain has been counted. The ~275 million neurons are estimated from body size using a fish brain-scaling rule. The weight note in the data was copied from an old neuron note. Bycatch isn't modelled for tuna, though longline and purse-seine tuna fisheries do catch sharks, turtles and juvenile fish, so its harm is probably understated.

name: Shrimp (Wild)
notes:
Wild trawl-caught shrimp, nutrition from USDA raw shrimp. It's tagged 'wild' for the Over-Hunting slider.

The big issue is bycatch. Shrimp trawls catch about 5.7 kg of other sea life per kg of shrimp landed, mostly small fish that are discarded dead (WWF; Henriksson 2015 gives 2–10 kg). Sardines stand in for those discarded fish when counting the deaths. Each shrimp is only ~18 g with 60% meat, so ~90 shrimp die per kg as well.

Shrimp neurons are estimated at up to 1 million, a conservative upper end. Emissions are trawler diesel, ~3.2 kg CO2 per kg (Poore & Nemecek, Parker 2018). No land or feed.

Some vitamins come from a stand-in USDA record (Crustaceans, shrimp, mixed species, raw (may contain additives to retain moisture)) because the main record doesn't list them.

name: Shrimp (Farmed)
notes:
Pond-farmed shrimp (mostly whiteleg shrimp, Penaeus vannamei), nutrition from USDA raw shrimp. Many shrimp ponds in Southeast Asia and Latin America replaced mangrove forest. That land-use change is the biggest single emission source, and it's carried in the large direct-CO2 figure (~18.6 kg per kg) derived from Poore & Nemecek's farmed-prawn total (~26.9).

Ponds also give off methane and nitrous oxide from rotting feed and waste (Henriksson 2015). Feed per kg is ~0.75 kg soy, 0.5 kg wheat, 0.34 kg fishmeal and 0.07 kg fish oil. The fishmeal and oil mean wild anchoveta are killed for the feed, counted as a direct kill.

Each shrimp is ~18 g with 60% meat, so ~90 shrimp die per kg. Neurons are estimated at up to 1 million each.

Some vitamins come from a stand-in USDA record (Crustaceans, shrimp, mixed species, raw (may contain additives to retain moisture)) because the main record doesn't list them.

name: Sardines (Wild)
notes:
Wild sardines and pilchards, caught by purse-seine nets. Nutrition from USDA. Tagged 'wild' for the Over-Hunting slider.

Sardines are among the lowest-emission animal foods: purse seines catch dense schools with little fuel, ~1.5 kg CO2 per kg (Poore & Nemecek's small-pelagic range). No land or feed. A large share of the world sardine catch is actually reduced to fishmeal rather than eaten, so availability overstates sardines eaten as food.

Each sardine is ~100 g with 75% edible, so about 13 die per kg. Neurons (~29 million) are estimated from body size using a fish brain-scaling rule. Bycatch is set at 0.1 kg of tuna per kg of sardines, but no derivation is recorded for that number. Sardines are also used as the stand-in species for discarded bycatch in the shrimp and cod entries.

name: Tilapia (Farmed)
notes:
Farmed Nile tilapia, nutrition from USDA. Tilapia eat a mostly plant-based feed (soy, corn, wheat, with a little fishmeal), so they're among the lowest-impact farmed fish. Poore & Nemecek give ~3.2 kg CO2e per kg in total.

Only about a third of the fish is fillet (0.33 of live weight), so each kg of fillet takes ~5.5 kg of feed and ~4 fish. Pond methane and nitrous oxide are small. Land is only the feed cropland.

Neurons (~57 million) are estimated from body size (0.7 kg) using a fish brain-scaling rule; no tilapia count exists.

name: Mussels (Farmed)
notes:
Farmed blue mussels, grown on ropes. Nutrition from USDA. Mussels filter-feed on wild plankton, so there's no feed, fertilizer or farmland. Emissions are boat fuel and gear. Two methods agree closely: a bivalve LCA median (392 kg CO2e per tonne shell-on ÷ 27% meat) and MacLeod et al. 2020's per-protein figure, ~1.3–1.45 kg CO2e per kg meat.

Bivalves have no brain, only small clusters of nerve cells, so neurons are estimated at about 17,000. Each mussel gives only ~3.2 g of meat, so roughly 300 die per kg.

Body weight for the intelligence score is standardized (changed 2026-10-01). Shells are a very different share of each bivalve's weight (oysters ~90%, mussels ~73%). So all three bivalves get their meat weight × 6.53, the average shell-plus-meat ratio, rather than shell-on weight. That stops oysters looking less sentient just because of heavy shells. Meat per animal still uses the real 27% meat yield.

name: Octopus (Wild)
notes:
Wild common octopus, nutrition from USDA raw octopus. Tagged 'wild' for the Over-Hunting slider.

Octopuses are by far the most neuron-rich seafood here: ~500 million neurons (Young 1963, a direct count), about two-thirds in the arms, all counted. That's more than a chicken or duck. Each octopus is ~2 kg with ~80% edible, so fewer than one dies per kg, but each death counts heavily.

Emissions average two fishing methods. Pots are 3.1 kg CO2e per kg landed (Almeida et al. 2022, Portugal) ÷ 80% edible ≈ 3.9. Trawling is at least double that (≈ 7.75, a lower bound). Much of the world catch (NW Africa, Asia) is trawled. Bycatch isn't modelled, which understates harm for trawled octopus. Availability is FAO's world octopus catch (~377 kt live weight) × 80% edible.

name: Halibut (Wild)

Emissions use Parker et al. 2018's demersal-fish average (2.4 kg CO2e per kg landed) ÷ 34% fillet yield ≈ 7 kg per kg fillet. That's a trawl-weighted average, so longline halibut are probably lower. The 34% yield is Greenland halibut's, the only halibut in FAO TP 309. Discards use the same 9.6% demersal rate as cod, an upper bound for longlines.

Landed fish are assumed ~15 kg (an estimate; Pacific halibut reach 500 lb). Halibut live 50+ years, so each death counts against a long life. Neurons (~168 million) are estimated from body size.

name: Mahi-Mahi (Wild)
notes:

No species-specific emissions figure exists, so the tuna longline value (3.9 kg CO2e/kg) and Parker et al. 2018's pelagic average (1.9 ÷ 46% yield = 4.1) are both used. Bycatch isn't modelled. Edible yield (46%) borrows Japanese amberjack's estimate from FAO TP 309.

A catch is typically 7–13 kg (Wikipedia), so 10 kg is used. Mahi-mahi mature in months and live only ~4 years. Neurons (~146 million) are estimated from body size. USDA doesn't report vitamins D, E and K for mahi-mahi; those are guesses copied from haddock.

name: Mackerel (Wild)
notes:
Wild mackerel (Atlantic, chub and blue mackerel), nutrition from USDA (Atlantic mackerel). Tagged 'wild' for the Over-Hunting slider. Caught by purse seine and midwater trawl.

Emissions copy the small-pelagic value used for sardines (1.5 kg CO2e/kg), as does bycatch. Edible yield is the 54% skinless fillet from FAO TP 309.

A mackerel is ~0.5 kg (NOAA: up to 2.2 lb, up to 20 years). Neurons (~51 million) are estimated from body size. Mackerel is oily: high in omega-3 and vitamin B12, but also saturated fat.

source.title: Different ways of evolving tool-using brains in teleosts and amniotes (Communications Biology, 2024; PMC10786859)
source.note: Mackerel (Wild) — neuron_count (ESTIMATE, no direct count exists for this species). Method: (1) brain mass from body mass using the ray-finned fish scaling brain ∝ body^0.5 (source 384), anchored on brown trout (177.15 g body, 354.73 mg brain): 500 g body → 354.73 × (500/177.15)^0.5 = 596 mg brain. (2) total brain cells from brain mass using a fit to isotropic-fractionator counts in medaka, zebrafish, Astyanax and trout (source 384): 1.669 × 596^0.706 = 152.0 M cells. (3) neurons = 1/3 of cells, from tilapia's measured 2 non-neuronal cells per neuron (source 385): 50.7 M neurons.

name: Squid (Wild)
notes:
Wild squid (calamari), nutrition from USDA mixed species. Tagged 'wild' for the Over-Hunting slider. Caught by jigging and trawl.

Squid are neuron-rich: a bigfin reef squid has ~500 million neurons (Chung et al. 2020), the same as an octopus, and that figure is used for all squid (confidence 2; commercial species differ in size). Squid live about a year.

Edible yield is FAO TP 309's 67% for squids. Emissions are Parker et al. 2018's pelagic average (1.9 kg CO2e per kg landed) ÷ 67% ≈ 2.8; no squid-specific figure was found. Bycatch isn't modelled. Availability uses every FAO species with 'squid' in the name, which includes bobtail squids and cuttlefish.

A squid is ~0.3 kg (Japanese flying squid reach 0.5 kg; this is an estimate).

name: Crab (Wild)
notes:
Wild crab, nutrition from USDA (blue crab, raw meat). Tagged 'wild' for the Over-Hunting slider. Most crab is caught in pots and traps.

No crab count of neurons exists, so ~1 million is used, the upper end of the range assumed for shrimp (crustacean nervous systems are far smaller than fish or octopus). Confidence 1.

Emissions copy wild shrimp's P&N crustacean figure (3.2 kg CO2e/kg); crab pot fisheries probably differ, but no crab figure was found. Bycatch isn't modelled. Edible yield (15%) is an estimate of picked meat per live crab; no source was checked. A blue crab is ~1/3 lb (NOAA).

USDA doesn't report vitamins D, E and K for crab; those are copied from raw mixed-species shrimp.

name: Lobster (Wild)
notes:
Wild lobster, nutrition from USDA (spiny lobster, raw meat). Tagged 'wild' for the Over-Hunting slider. Most of the world's catch is spiny lobster; American and European lobster are caught in traps.

No lobster count of neurons exists, so ~1 million is used, the upper end of the range assumed for shrimp. Confidence 1. Lobsters live a very long time (American lobster possibly ~100 years, NOAA) but each is eaten at 5–10 years.

Emissions copy wild shrimp's P&N crustacean figure (3.2 kg CO2e/kg), which probably understates lobster: lobster pot fisheries are fuel-hungry per kg of meat. Confidence 1. Bycatch isn't modelled. Edible yield (30%) is an estimate; no source was checked. A lobster is ~0.7 kg (NOAA: American lobster up to 44 lb).

USDA doesn't report vitamins D, E and K for lobster; those are copied from raw mixed-species shrimp.
